symptoms: red or brownish patches (especially on flexural areas)
symptoms often flare in winter or with stress
guidance: Use gentle, fragrance-free moisturizers multiple times daily. Avoid harsh soaps and hot water. Topical corticosteroids are first-line for flares. For moderate-severe cases, calcineurin inhibitors or biologics (dupilumab) may be needed. Avoid known triggers. Free consultations are available at government dermatology clinics.

symptoms: greasy, yellowish scales on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, chest
may worsen in winter or with stress
guidance: Use medicated shampoos containing ketoconazole, zinc pyrithione, or selenium sulfide. For facial involvement, use antifungal cream (ketoconazole). In severe cases, topical corticosteroids may be used. Maintenance therapy is often needed.
precautions: Wash hair regularly with anti-dandruff shampoos
If scalp lesions persist, see a dermatologist
Do not scratch – can cause secondary infection

symptoms: facial redness (erythema) over cheeks, nose, chin
thickening of skin (rhinophyma) in severe cases
guidance: Avoid triggers: sun exposure, spicy foods, alcohol, and extreme temperatures. Topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, or ivermectin are first-line. Oral antibiotics (doxycycline) for moderate-severe. Laser therapy for telangiectasia. Protect skin with sunscreen (SPF 50+).
precautions: Avoid hot beverages and spicy foods
Consult a dermatologist for prescription treatments

symptoms: small, red, scaly papules around the mouth, nose, and eyes
spares the vermilion border of the lips
guidance: Stop use of topical steroids (they can worsen). Use topical metronidazole, erythromycin, or pimecrolimus. Avoid heavy creams, occlusive cosmetics, and fluoride toothpaste (may help). In severe cases, oral antibiotics (doxycycline).
precautions: Do not use topical steroids on the face

guidance: Over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid, or retinoids (adapalene). For moderate-severe, prescription topical retinoids, antibiotics, or oral isotretinoin. Hormonal therapy (OCPs, spironolactone) for women. Lifestyle: avoid picking, use non-comedogenic products.
precautions: Do not squeeze or pop pimples
If on isotretinoin, avoid pregnancy (contraception mandatory)

symptoms: recurrent, painful, deep-seated inflamed nodules and abscesses in intertriginous areas (axillae, groin, breasts, buttocks)
guidance: Weight loss and smoking cessation are critical. Topical clindamycin, oral antibiotics (tetracyclines, rifampicin), and biologics (adalimumab) for moderate-severe. Surgical deroofing or excision for sinus tracts. Free biologics are available at some government hospitals. Warm compresses help.

symptoms: pruritic, polygonal, flat-topped, violaceous papules and plaques
often on wrists, ankles, lower back, and flexor surfaces
Wickham's striae (white, lacy lines on surface)
Koebner phenomenon (lesions at sites of trauma)
guidance: Topical corticosteroids are first-line. For extensive disease, phototherapy (UVB) or systemic corticosteroids. Oral involvement may need topical steroids or tacrolimus. Avoid trauma to skin. Regular follow-up to monitor for malignant transformation (rare).
precautions: If oral lesions persist, see a dentist/ENT

symptoms: herald patch (large pink patch, often on trunk)
followed by multiple smaller oval pink/scaly patches on trunk and proximal limbs (Christmas tree pattern)
guidance: Self-limiting (6-8 weeks). Treatment is symptomatic: antihistamines for itching, and UVB phototherapy for severe or prolonged cases. Avoid using topical steroids on the face. Reassurance is key.
precautions: If itching is severe, use antihistamines
Do not apply strong steroids without advice
Monitor for resolution – if persistent, see a dermatologist

symptoms: annular, scaly, erythematous plaque with central clearing
guidance: Topical antifungals (clotrimazole, terbinafine, miconazole) for 2-4 weeks. For extensive or tinea capitis, oral terbinafine or griseofulvin. Keep the area dry and avoid sharing personal items.
precautions: Do not share towels or clothing
If on oral antifungals, monitor liver function

symptoms: itchy, red, scaly rash in the groin and inner thighs
guidance: Apply topical antifungal cream (clotrimazole, terbinafine) twice daily for 2-4 weeks. Keep the area dry, wear loose cotton underwear, and avoid tight clothing. If extensive, oral antifungals may be needed.
precautions: Do not use steroid creams alone – can worsen

symptoms: scaly, itchy, peeling skin between toes
guidance: Topical antifungal creams (clotrimazole, terbinafine) for 2-4 weeks. Keep feet dry, wear cotton socks, and avoid walking barefoot in public places. If severe, oral terbinafine. Secondary bacterial infection may need antibiotics.

symptoms: scaly, itchy patch on the scalp
guidance: This requires systemic antifungal therapy (oral terbinafine, griseofulvin, or itraconazole) for 6-8 weeks. Topical treatments are not effective. Selenium sulfide shampoo can reduce shedding. Monitor liver function. Free treatment at government hospitals.
precautions: Do not share combs, hats, or towels

symptoms: hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on trunk, neck, and upper arms
guidance: Topical antifungal (selenium sulfide shampoo, ketoconazole, or terbinafine) applied daily for 1-2 weeks. For extensive disease, oral antifungals (fluconazole, itraconazole). Pigmentation may take months to normalize. Recurrence is common.
precautions: Use antifungal wash once monthly for prevention
If on oral, complete the course
Sun exposure may make patches more visible – use sunscreen

symptoms: moist, erythematous, itchy rash in skin folds (axillae, groin, under breasts, buttocks)
often associated with diabetes or obesity
guidance: Keep skin folds dry. Topical antifungal (clotrimazole, miconazole) with or without low-potency steroid for inflammation. In severe cases, oral fluconazole. Treat underlying diabetes and lose weight.
precautions: Dry skin folds thoroughly after bathing

symptoms: small, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication (dimple)
guidance: Usually self-limiting (6-18 months). For cosmetic or to prevent spread, options include cryotherapy, curettage, or topical agents (cantharidin). In immunocompromised, may be more extensive. Avoid scratching.
precautions: Do not share towels or clothing
Cover lesions in children to prevent autoinoculation
In adults, sexual transmission may occur

symptoms: firm, rough, flesh-colored or greyish papule with a cauliflower-like surface
most common on hands, fingers, around nails
guidance: Topical salicylic acid, cryotherapy, or curettage. Recurrence is common. Avoid picking warts. If persistent, see a dermatologist. In children, often resolve spontaneously.
precautions: Do not bite or pick warts
If on feet, wear comfortable shoes
Do not use the same file on normal skin
If multiple or growing, seek medical advice

symptoms: painful, callus-like lesion on the sole of the foot
pain on pressure (like a stone in the shoe)
guidance: Treatment options: salicylic acid plasters, cryotherapy, laser, or surgical excision. Avoid self-treatment with acids if diabetic. If painful, see a podiatrist or dermatologist.
precautions: Do not walk barefoot in public places

symptoms: clusters of painful, fluid-filled blisters on lips, mouth, or genitals
guidance: Topical acyclovir or penciclovir can reduce duration if started early. For frequent recurrences, prophylactic oral antivirals (acyclovir, valacyclovir). Avoid triggers (sun, stress). Do not share lip balms.
precautions: Do not share utensils or lip products

symptoms: painful, vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution (unilateral)
burning, tingling, or neuralgic pain before rash
guidance: Antiviral (acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir) within 72 hours of rash onset to reduce severity and post-herpetic neuralgia. Pain management with NSAIDs, gabapentin, or antidepressants. Zoster vaccine prevents or reduces severity. Keep rash covered to prevent transmission.
precautions: Avoid contact with pregnant women and immunocompromised

symptoms: red sores that quickly rupture and form honey-colored crusts
often on face, arms, or legs
guidance: Topical mupirocin for limited cases. Extensive or deep lesions need oral antibiotics (dicloxacillin, cephalexin). Good hygiene: wash with soap, keep lesions covered. If recurrent, check for nasal carriage.
precautions: Do not share towels or clothing

guidance: Medical emergency – requires oral or IV antibiotics (cephalexin, clindamycin, or penicillin). Elevate the affected limb. Monitor for abscess or sepsis. Do not delay – can lead to bacteremia.
precautions: If redness spreads despite antibiotics, seek emergency
Avoid using steroid creams on cellulitis

symptoms: well-demarcated, raised, fiery red plaque on face or legs
guidance: This is a superficial cellulitis usually caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. Treat with systemic antibiotics (penicillin or cephalexin). Elevate the affected area. Hospitalisation for severe cases. Recurrence is common; consider prophylaxis.
precautions: Treat fungal infections between toes (portal of entry)

symptoms: severe pain out of proportion to skin findings
guidance: This is a surgical emergency. Call 108 immediately. Requires urgent surgical debridement and IV antibiotics. Do not delay. High mortality. Hospitalisation is critical.
precautions: Do not delay – early debridement saves lives
If you have a wound with severe pain, seek care

symptoms: small, red, tender papules or pustules around hair follicles
commonly on scalp, face, axillae, buttocks
guidance: For bacterial: topical mupirocin or clindamycin; for extensive, oral antibiotics. For fungal: antifungal. Keep area clean, avoid shaving. Prevention: good hygiene, loose clothing.
precautions: If recurrent, check for nasal carriage of bacteria

symptoms: tender, red, swollen nodule (furuncle) that becomes fluctuant (pus-filled)
multiple furuncles coalescing into carbuncle (more extensive)
commonly on neck, face, axillae, buttocks
guidance: Warm compresses to promote drainage. Incision and drainage if fluctuant. Antibiotics if systemic symptoms. Recurrent boils may need decolonization (mupirocin nasal, chlorhexidine washes).

symptoms: red, moist, macerated rash in skin folds (groin, axillae, under breasts, abdominal folds)
guidance: Keep skin folds dry. Use barrier creams (zinc oxide) and antifungal or antibacterial agents as needed. Lose weight if obese. Wear moisture-wicking clothing.
precautions: Dry skin folds thoroughly after bathing
Avoid steroid creams alone – can worsen fungal

symptoms: result of chronic scratching and rubbing
commonly on ankles, wrists, neck, and vulva
guidance: Break the itch-scratch cycle. Topical corticosteroids and antihistamines. Behavioral modification (avoid scratching). Treat underlying psychological stress. Sometimes intralesional steroids.
precautions: If associated with eczema, treat eczema

symptoms: intensely itchy nodules (pruritic) on arms, legs, and trunk
often in atopic individuals or with systemic disease (CKD, liver disease)
guidance: Treat underlying condition. Topical steroids, intralesional steroids, phototherapy, and systemic medications (antidepressants, anticonvulsants) for severe pruritus. Avoid scratching – use occlusive dressings.

symptoms: burrows (thin, wavy, greyish lines) in finger webs, wrists, elbows, axillae, genitals
guidance: Topical permethrin 5% cream applied from neck down, left overnight, washed off in morning. Treat all household members simultaneously. Wash clothing and bedding in hot water. If persistent, may need ivermectin. Pruritus may take weeks to resolve.
precautions: Treat all family members at the same time
Wash all linen and clothing in hot water
If pruritus persists, may need repeat treatment
Do not use steroids without scabicide

symptoms: visible nits (eggs) attached to hair shafts (especially behind ears and nape)
guidance: Topical permethrin 1% or pyrethrin shampoo, leave for 10 minutes, rinse, and comb with a fine-toothed comb. Repeat in 7-10 days. Wash bedding and clothing in hot water. All household contacts should be checked.
precautions: Do not share combs, hats, or hair accessories
Wash bedding and clothing in hot water
Treat all family members if infested
If resistant, use malathion or ivermectin

guidance: Apply permethrin 1% cream or pyrethrin shampoo to pubic area, leave for 10 minutes, rinse. Also treat eyelashes with petrolatum (twice daily for 8 days). Sexual partners should be treated. Wash clothes in hot water.
precautions: Do not share towels or clothing
If eyelash involvement, do not use pesticides – use petroleum jelly

symptoms: intensely itchy, red, linear or serpiginous track on the skin (often feet, buttocks)
occurs after walking on contaminated soil or sand (hookworm larvae)
track progresses a few mm per day
guidance: Oral ivermectin or albendazole is effective. Topical thiabendazole. Antihistamines for itching. Prevention: wear shoes in tropical areas.
precautions: Avoid walking barefoot on sandy beaches
If you have a track, see a doctor
Do not scratch – can cause infection

symptoms: chronic, painless ulcer with raised, rolled edges
may have central crust or scab
history of travel to endemic areas (India, Middle East)
guidance: Treatment depends on species: topical paromomycin, intralesional antimony, or systemic amphotericin B. In India, mucosal disease is rare. Free treatment under government programs. Avoid secondary infection.
precautions: Prevent sandfly bites (bed nets, insect repellent)
Wear long sleeves in endemic areas
If ulcer persists, seek medical care

symptoms: hypopigmented or erythematous patches with loss of sensation (anesthesia)
guidance: Free multi-drug therapy (MDT) is available at all PHCs and government hospitals under the National Leprosy Eradication Programme. Treatment lasts 6-12 months. Early diagnosis prevents disability. All cases are notifiable. Contacts should be examined.
precautions: Do not ignore patches with loss of sensation
Monitor for nerve damage and reactions (steroids may be needed)

symptoms: slowly progressive, red-brown plaques with an apple-jelly colour on diascopy
guidance: Tuberculous skin infections are treated with standard anti-TB drugs (DOTS regimen) for 6-9 months. Free treatment under RNTCP. Suspect if there is a history of TB exposure. Confirm with biopsy and PCR.

symptoms: painless, cold abscess in cervical lymph nodes or skin overlying infected nodes
skin becomes adherent, then ulcerates with undermined edges
guidance: Standard anti-TB therapy (DOTS) is curative. Surgical drainage may be needed for large abscesses. Free treatment is available.
precautions: Do not delay surgery if needed

symptoms: rough, scaly, erythematous papules or plaques on sun-exposed skin
often on face, scalp, ears, dorsa of hands
precancerous lesion (risk of squamous cell carcinoma)
guidance: Treatment: cryotherapy, topical 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, or diclofenac. Sun protection is crucial. If lesions are numerous, photodynamic therapy. Biopsy any lesion that becomes indurated or ulcerated.
precautions: Avoid sun exposure between 10 AM-4 PM

symptoms: slow-growing, pearly, shiny bump with telangiectasia
guidance: Treatment: surgical excision is the mainstay; options include Mohs micrographic surgery (best for face), cryotherapy, radiotherapy, or topical imiquimod for superficial lesions. Early detection is key. Free surgery under PMJAY.
precautions: Sun protection is the best prevention
If you have a suspicious lesion, see a dermatologist

symptoms: firm, red, scaly plaque or nodule
on sun-exposed skin, but also on scars, burn sites
guidance: Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs surgery for high-risk areas. Radiation therapy for non-surgical candidates. Follow-up for metastases. Prevention: sun protection, avoid smoking.
precautions: If you have a history of immunosuppression, monitor
If lesion grows rapidly, seek care

symptoms: ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border irregular, Colour variegated, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving (changing)
may be nodular, superficial spreading, or lentigo maligna
can arise in pre-existing mole or de novo
guidance: Melanoma is the deadliest skin cancer. Early diagnosis saves lives. Surgical excision with wide margins is primary. Sentinel node biopsy for staging. Immunotherapy and targeted therapy for advanced disease. Free care under PMJAY. Regular skin self-exams and professional mole checks.
precautions: If you have a family history, get regular skin checks
If a mole changes, see a dermatologist immediately

guidance: No treatment needed – it is benign. If cosmetic concern, cryotherapy, curettage, or laser. Reassurance is important. Do not pick or irritate.
precautions: If a lesion changes rapidly or bleeds, get it checked
Use sunscreen – they are not sun-induced

guidance: Benign – no treatment needed. If growing or symptomatic, excision may be done for diagnosis. Reassure that it is not cancer.
precautions: If multiple, may be associated with lupus

symptoms: raised, firm, smooth, shiny scar tissue
extends beyond the original wound (keloid) or stays within (hypertrophic)
more common in darker skin types
guidance: Prevention: avoid unnecessary surgery, use silicone gel sheets on healing wounds. Treatment: intralesional steroids, cryotherapy, laser, radiation, or surgical excision with postoperative steroid injections. Silicone sheeting is the mainstay.
precautions: If you have a history of keloids, avoid elective surgery
If keloid is growing, see a dermatologist

symptoms: colour similar to skin or slightly darker
common in neck, axillae, groin, and eyelids
more common with obesity and diabetes
guidance: Benign – no treatment needed. If bothersome, removal by snipping (cautery), cryotherapy, or ligation. Associated with insulin resistance – may indicate screening for diabetes.
precautions: If a tag changes colour or bleeds, see a doctor
Do not self-remove – can bleed or get infected
If you have many, check blood sugar

symptoms: rough, small, red or white bumps on upper arms, thighs, buttocks
guidance: Moisturizers with keratolytic agents (urea, lactic acid, salicylic acid) help. Topical retinoids may improve appearance. No cure, but condition often improves with age. Avoid dry skin.

symptoms: dry, scaly skin with fine white or brown scales
worse in winter, improves in summer
guidance: Regular moisturization (after bathing) with emollients containing urea, lactic acid, or salicylic acid. Avoid long hot baths. Topical retinoids for severe cases. Gene therapy is not yet available.
precautions: If scaling is severe, see a dermatologist

symptoms: generalized redness (erythema) and scaling of >90% of body surface
can be caused by psoriasis, eczema, drug reaction, or lymphoma
guidance: This is a medical emergency. Hospitalisation is needed. Treat the underlying cause (drug withdrawal, psoriasis, etc.). Supportive care: emollients, corticosteroids, and monitoring of fluid/electrolytes. If drug-induced, stop the drug.
precautions: Do not delay – erythroderma can be life-threatening
If you develop generalized redness, seek emergency care

symptoms: blistering and detachment of skin (Nikolsky sign)
rash begins as target-like lesions, then spreads
guidance: This is a medical emergency. Stop the offending drug immediately. Hospitalise in an ICU or burns unit. Supportive care: fluid resuscitation, wound care, pain management. Systemic corticosteroids are controversial; IVIG may be used. Ophthalmology consultation is critical.
precautions: If you have a severe drug reaction with mucosal involvement, call 108 immediately
Do not take any more of the suspected drug
Eye care is essential to prevent blindness
If you survive, avoid the causative drug forever

symptoms: target-like (bull's eye) lesions on extremities (hands, feet, palms, soles)
often triggered by herpes simplex or drugs
guidance: If herpes-associated, treat with antivirals. If drug-induced, stop the drug. Supportive care: antihistamines, pain relief. Severe cases (Stevens-Johnson) need urgent care.
precautions: If you have recurrent erythema multiforme, consider prophylactic acyclovir
If mucosal involvement, see a doctor

symptoms: tender, red, subcutaneous nodules on shins (bilateral)
associated with infections (strep, TB), drugs, or inflammatory bowel disease
guidance: Treat the underlying cause. NSAIDs for pain. Bed rest and leg elevation. Potassium iodide may help. If recurrent, investigate for sarcoidosis, TB, or IBD. Biopsy is diagnostic.
precautions: If you have tender nodules on shins, see a doctor
If you have associated symptoms, investigate

symptoms: ring-shaped, skin-coloured or red papules, often on dorsa of hands and feet
guidance: Usually no treatment needed – often resolves spontaneously. Topical steroids or calcineurin inhibitors may be used for cosmetic concern. If extensive, phototherapy or antimalarials. Screen for diabetes.
precautions: If you have a ring-shaped rash, get evaluated
Do not use potent steroids without advice

symptoms: intensely itchy, grouped papulovesicles on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks)
guidance: Diagnosis: skin biopsy (direct immunofluorescence shows IgA deposits). Treatment: dapsone (rapid relief) and a strict gluten-free diet (long-term control). Associated with celiac disease – monitor for gastrointestinal symptoms.
precautions: Monitor for hemolytic anemia (G6PD test before starting dapsone)
If you have celiac, follow diet

symptoms: painful, flaccid blisters and erosions on skin and mucous membranes (mouth, throat, genitals)
positive Nikolsky sign (skin shears with pressure)
guidance: This is a serious autoimmune blistering disease. Treatment: systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone) and immunosuppressants (azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab). Hospitalisation may be needed. Free rituximab is available at some government centres. Careful wound care and infection prevention.
precautions: Do not delay treatment – can be fatal
If you have oral ulcers that don't heal, see a dermatologist
Take steroids as prescribed – do not stop suddenly

symptoms: tense, large blisters on flexural areas (groin, axillae, lower abdomen)
guidance: Treatment: topical or systemic corticosteroids. In mild cases, topical steroids suffice. For extensive disease, oral steroids and immunosuppressants (methotrexate, mycophenolate). Rituximab for refractory cases. Monitor for infections and side effects.
precautions: Take steroids as prescribed – taper slowly
If blisters rupture, keep clean to prevent infection
Monitor for side effects of steroids
If on immunosuppressants, avoid live vaccines

symptoms: intensely itchy, urticarial plaques and blisters in the second or third trimester of pregnancy
resolves postpartum, but may flare at delivery
guidance: Treatment: topical corticosteroids for mild cases; oral prednisolone for severe. Monitor fetal growth. Postpartum may flare. Refer to dermatologist and obstetrician. Usually resolves after delivery but may recur.
precautions: If you develop itchy blisters in pregnancy, see a dermatologist

symptoms: well-circumscribed, ivory-white, indurated plaques with a violaceous border
guidance: Morphea is usually self-limiting. Topical corticosteroids, calcipotriene, or tacrolimus may help. Phototherapy (UVA) for extensive lesions. If linear morphea (en coup de sabre), may need systemic immunosuppression. No internal organ involvement.
precautions: If you have a patch of hard skin, see a dermatologist
If linear on face, ophthalmology check

symptoms: facial skin becomes taut, microstomia (small mouth)
guidance: Management: skin care, avoid cold, vasodilators for Raynaud's. Immunosuppression (methotrexate, mycophenolate) for skin involvement. Pulmonary and renal screening. Multidisciplinary care. Free immunosuppressants at government hospitals.

symptoms: malar rash (butterfly rash on cheeks and nose) – acute
discoid lupus: scaly, coin-shaped plaques with scarring and pigment changes
subacute cutaneous: annular or psoriasiform lesions
guidance: Sun protection is critical. Topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, or antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine) for cutaneous lupus. Systemic therapy for systemic involvement. Avoid sun exposure – use SPF 50+.
precautions: If you have discoid lesions, monitor for scarring

symptoms: Gottron's papules (erythematous plaques over knuckles, elbows)
guidance: Sun protection. Topical steroids. Systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants (methotrexate, mycophenolate) for muscle involvement. Screen for malignancy (ovarian, lung). Refer to rheumatology.
precautions: If you have muscle weakness, seek care

symptoms: fragile skin that blisters and peels on sun-exposed areas (hands, face)
urine turns reddish (pink) on exposure to light
guidance: Avoid alcohol, oestrogen, and iron supplements. Phlebotomy (to reduce iron) and low-dose hydroxychloroquine are effective. Sun protection. Treat underlying causes (hepatitis C, haemochromatosis).
precautions: Avoid sun exposure – use protective clothing
If you have hepatitis C, treat it
If you have blisters, see a dermatologist

symptoms: acute, painful photosensitivity (burning, stinging, itching) on sun-exposed skin, minutes after sun exposure
redness, swelling, later crusting and scarring
guidance: Sun avoidance and protective clothing are key. Beta-carotene may reduce photosensitivity. Afamelanotide (a melanocortin analogue) is used in some countries. Monitor for liver function. Refer to dermatology and hepatology.
precautions: Avoid sun exposure – wear protective clothing
If you have pain after sun exposure, seek care

symptoms: sudden, patchy hair loss (well-circumscribed round/oval bald patches)
exclamation mark hairs (tapered at the base) at the periphery
may progress to totalis (scalp) or universalis (whole body)
guidance: Topical corticosteroids, intralesional steroids, or minoxidil. For extensive disease, systemic corticosteroids, contact immunotherapy (DPCP), or JAK inhibitors (available at some centres). Emotional support is crucial. Spontaneous regrowth is common.
precautions: Do not panic – many cases regrow
If on systemic steroids, monitor side effects
If you have associated thyroid disease, check
Wear wigs or hats if desired

symptoms: progressive hair thinning (frontotemporal in males, crown in both)
guidance: Topical minoxidil (2-5%) and oral finasteride (men) are FDA-approved. Low-level laser therapy and hair transplant for advanced cases. In women, spironolactone may be used. Early treatment is best.
precautions: Start treatment early for best results
Minoxidil takes 4-6 months to show effect
Finasteride is not for women of childbearing age
If you have side effects, discuss with doctor

symptoms: diffuse hair shedding (increased hair fall) 2-3 months after a triggering event (fever, childbirth, stress, surgery)
guidance: Reassurance – it is self-limiting. Treat the underlying cause. Good nutrition (iron, protein, vitamins). Hair regrowth typically occurs within 6 months. If persistent, check iron, thyroid, and ferritin.
precautions: Do not panic – it will regrow
If shedding persists, see a dermatologist

symptoms: excessive sweating beyond what is needed for temperature regulation
guidance: Topical aluminium chloride antiperspirants, iontophoresis, botulinum toxin injections, oral anticholinergics, or sympathectomy (for severe cases). Lifestyle: wear breathable fabrics, manage stress. Free botox may be available at some government centres.
precautions: If you have secondary hyperhidrosis, treat the cause

symptoms: unpleasant body odour (often from apocrine glands in axillae, groin)
associated with bacterial breakdown of sweat
may be present despite good hygiene
guidance: Improve hygiene: wash with antibacterial soaps, use antiperspirants, wear breathable fabrics. If severe, topical antibiotics (clindamycin) or botulinum toxin (reduces sweating). Dietary changes may help (avoid strong-smelling foods).
precautions: If related to systemic disease, treat it

symptoms: red, itchy, swollen patches on toes, fingers, ears, nose
after exposure to cold and damp (not freezing)
pain, burning, ulceration in severe cases
guidance: Keep warm – wear gloves, thick socks. Avoid rapid warming. Use topical corticosteroids for itching. In severe cases, vasodilators (nifedipine). Prevention: warm clothing, avoid cold exposure.

symptoms: partial- or full-thickness skin loss (stages II-IV)
usually over bony prominences (sacrum, heels, elbows)
guidance: Prevention: turn bedridden patients every 2 hours, use pressure-relieving mattresses, keep skin clean and dry. Treatment: wound care (debridement, dressings), offloading, and treatment of infection. Severe cases need surgery.

symptoms: chronic, shallow, irregular ulcer on the medial leg above the ankle
guidance: Compression therapy (elastic bandages or stockings) is the mainstay. Wound care with hydrocolloids or foam dressings. Elevate legs. Treat varicose veins if needed. Infection requires antibiotics. Regular follow-up.

symptoms: scaly, itchy, erythematous patches on lower legs (especially medial malleolus)
guidance: Compression stockings, leg elevation, and moisturizers. Topical steroids for inflammation. Treat underlying venous disease (sclerotherapy or surgery). If ulcer, wound care. Avoid scratching.
precautions: If ulcer, see a wound care specialist

symptoms: may be associated with atopic dermatitis or ageing
guidance: Use thick emollients (petrolatum, ceramide-containing creams) after bathing. Avoid harsh soaps and hot water. Use a humidifier in winter. If itchy, use antihistamines. If severe, see a dermatologist.
precautions: If you have eczema, treat it

symptoms: intense itching in the perianal area
may be associated with pinworms, hemorrhoids, or excessive hygiene
guidance: Avoid aggressive wiping – use wet wipes or sitz baths. Use emollients and topical corticosteroids. Treat the underlying cause (deworming, hemorrhoids). Good perianal hygiene. Avoid irritants (spicy foods, caffeine).
precautions: If persistent, see a dermatologist or proctologist

symptoms: velvety, hyperpigmented, thickened plaques on flexural areas (neck, axillae, groin)
associated with insulin resistance, obesity, and diabetes
may be a sign of internal malignancy (if sudden onset)
guidance: Treat underlying insulin resistance (weight loss, exercise, metformin). If sudden or extensive, evaluate for malignancy (acanthosis nigricans maligna). Cosmetic treatments: topical retinoids, laser. Screen for diabetes.
precautions: If you have diabetes, control blood sugar
If sudden onset, see a doctor
Do not use skin-lightening creams without advice

symptoms: greasy, crusted, warty papules in seborrheic areas (face, chest, flexures)
may have nail changes (red and white longitudinal bands)
guidance: Topical retinoids, keratolytics, and sun protection. Severe cases: oral retinoids (acitretin). Genetic counselling. Avoid sweating and heat. Good skin care.
precautions: If on oral retinoids, monitor lipids and liver

symptoms: blistering and erosions in flexural areas (groin, axillae, neck)
worsened by heat, sweating, and friction
guidance: Topical corticosteroids, antibiotics, and emollients. Oral antibiotics (tetracycline) may help. In severe cases, dapsone or retinoids. Avoid friction and heat. Genetic counselling.

symptoms: fragile skin that blisters with minor trauma
blisters on hands, feet, elbows, knees (simplex), or widespread (dystrophic)
guidance: Wound care: gentle cleansing, non-adherent dressings, infection prevention. Avoid trauma. Good nutrition and pain management. Genetic counselling. Multidisciplinary care. Free dressings may be available at government hospitals.

symptoms: may have systemic symptoms (if mast cell activation)
guidance: Avoid triggers: heat, friction, stress, alcohol. Antihistamines are the mainstay. If systemic, may need mast cell stabilizers. Regular monitoring. In children, often resolves.
precautions: If you have flushing or hypotension, seek emergency (anaphylaxis risk)
If associated with systemic symptoms, see a specialist

symptoms: shiny, hyperpigmented, atrophic patches on shins (shin spots)
often multiple, small, round or oval
guidance: No specific treatment – good glycaemic control may prevent progression. Reassurance. Regular foot and skin checks. Prevent trauma.

symptoms: well-demarcated, yellow-brown, atrophic plaques with telangiectasia on shins
guidance: Glycaemic control. Topical steroids or intralesional steroids for active lesions. Protect from trauma. In ulceration, wound care. If extensive, consider phototherapy.
precautions: If ulceration, see a wound care specialist

symptoms: sudden eruption of small, red-yellow papules on buttocks, back, extremities
guidance: Treat the underlying hyperlipidemia (diet, statins, fibrates). Good glycaemic control if diabetic. Lesions may resolve with treatment. Monitor lipid profile.
precautions: If on fibrates, take as prescribed
If lesions are multiple, see a doctor

symptoms: yellowish, waxy papules on eyelids, larynx, and skin
guidance: Rare genetic disease. No specific treatment; symptom management. Speech therapy for hoarseness. Refer to dermatogenetics. Palliative care.

symptoms: often at sites of chronic irritation or inflammation
guidance: Biopsy to rule out malignancy. Treat underlying cause (remove irritant). May resolve with treatment. Regular follow-up.
precautions: If you have a persistent wart-like lesion, seek biopsy

symptoms: rapidly progressive, painful ulcer with a violaceous, undermined border
pathergy (new lesions at sites of trauma)
often associated with inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis, or haematological disorders
guidance: Treatment: systemic corticosteroids, cyclosporine, or infliximab. Wound care. Treat underlying disease. Avoid trauma. Immunosuppression is key.
precautions: Avoid trauma – can cause new lesions
If you have IBD, treat it
Do not use topical steroids alone

symptoms: patches, plaques, or tumours on skin
Sezary syndrome if erythroderma with circulating cells
guidance: Treatment: topical corticosteroids, phototherapy, bexarotene, or systemic chemotherapy. Referral to dermatology oncology. Early-stage disease has good prognosis. Free treatment at government oncology centres.
precautions: If you have persistent scaly patches, see a dermatologist

symptoms: purple, red, or brown papules/plaques on skin (often on legs, face, oral mucosa)
associated with HHV-8 and HIV infection
guidance: Treatment: antiretroviral therapy (ART) is the mainstay – often leads to regression. Local treatment with cryotherapy or radiation for cosmetic lesions. Systemic chemotherapy if visceral involvement. Free ART under NACO.
precautions: If lesions grow, see a dermatologist

symptoms: sudden, deep swelling of subcutaneous tissue, often around eyes, lips, hands, feet, and genitals
guidance: This is a medical emergency if the airway is involved – call 108 immediately. For allergic angioedema: antihistamines, corticosteroids, and epinephrine if anaphylaxis. For hereditary angioedema (C1 inhibitor deficiency): specific treatment (fresh frozen plasma, C1-INH concentrate, icatibant) – available at some centres.
precautions: If you have swelling of the tongue or throat, call emergency
If you have recurrent episodes, get evaluated (C1 inhibitor, C4, etc.)
Do not take ACE inhibitors if you have had angioedema
If hereditary, have an emergency plan

symptoms: diffuse, red maculopapular rash starting on trunk, spreading
occurs 7-14 days after starting a drug (penicillin, sulfonamides, etc.)
guidance: Stop the offending drug (if possible) and seek medical advice. Antihistamines and topical corticosteroids for symptom relief. If severe (fever, mucosal involvement), consider SJS/TEN and hospitalise. Use safe alternatives.
precautions: If you develop a rash after starting a drug, stop it and call your doctor
Do not scratch – can cause secondary infection
If you have mucosal involvement or blistering, seek emergency
Maintain a list of drug allergies

symptoms: well-circumscribed, round, red-violaceous plaque(s) that recur at the same site (often lips, genitals, hands) with each exposure to the offending drug
guidance: Identify and avoid the offending drug (commonly NSAIDs, tetracyclines, sulfonamides). Topical steroids for local inflammation. If severe, oral steroids. The hallmark is recurrence at the same site.
precautions: If you notice a recurring rash at the same spot, suspect a drug
Avoid that drug in the future
If you need to take it, ask for alternative
Keep a list of drug allergies

symptoms: palpable purpura (non-blanching, raised, red/purple spots) on lower legs
may have urticarial lesions, ulcers, or vesicles
often associated with infections, drugs, or autoimmune disease
guidance: Treat the underlying cause. If mild, NSAIDs. For severe (renal, GI) – systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants. Skin biopsy is diagnostic. Monitor renal function.
precautions: If you have purpuric spots, see a doctor
If you have joint pain or blood in urine, tell your doctor
Do not ignore – may be systemic

symptoms: small, red bumps or pustules on cheeks, nose, forehead of newborns
appears in the first few weeks of life
self-limiting, resolves within weeks to months
guidance: No treatment is needed – resolves spontaneously. Do not use acne creams or oils. If severe, may be due to maternal hormones. Reassurance.
precautions: Keep the skin clean with mild baby soap
If pustules are widespread, see a paediatrician

symptoms: transient, red macules and pustules on the face, trunk, and limbs of newborns
appears in the first few days of life
guidance: Reassurance – it is benign and self-limiting. No treatment needed. Avoid excessive washing or topical steroids.
precautions: If the baby is otherwise well, no worry
If pustules persist or the baby is sick, see a doctor

symptoms: more than 6 of >1.5 cm in post-pubertal individuals (or >0.5 cm in children) may indicate neurofibromatosis
guidance: If you have multiple café-au-lait spots, evaluate for NF1. Routine screening for other features (Lisch nodules, neurofibromas). Genetic counselling. Regular follow-up.
precautions: If you have >6 spots, see a geneticist
If you have high blood pressure, rule out renal artery stenosis

symptoms: unilateral, well-defined, hyperpigmented patch with hair growth (hypertrichosis)
often on the shoulder or upper chest
guidance: Benign – no treatment needed. If cosmetic concern, laser hair removal may help. Monitor for malignant transformation (very rare). Reassurance.
precautions: If the lesion changes, see a dermatologist
Do not pluck hairs (can cause folliculitis)
If you want hair removal, consider laser

symptoms: risk of melanoma (higher in giant nevi)
guidance: Small/medium CMN: low risk – monitor for changes. Giant CMN (>20 cm) has higher melanoma risk – consider prophylactic excision or regular surveillance. Dermatology follow-up. In case of change, biopsy.
precautions: If giant, see a dermatologist early
If there are satellite lesions, follow up

guidance: Topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors are first-line. Phototherapy (NB-UVB) for extensive disease. In stable cases, surgical transplantation. Sun protection is crucial – depigmented skin burns easily. Free phototherapy at some government hospitals.
precautions: Avoid sunburn – white patches burn easily
If you are on phototherapy, follow schedule

symptoms: hypopigmented, scaly patches on face (cheeks), arms
more common in children with atopic dermatitis
may be more noticeable in summer (surrounding tanning)
guidance: Usually self-limiting. Moisturizers and mild topical corticosteroids may help. Sun protection to reduce contrast. Reassurance – not permanent.
precautions: If associated with eczema, treat eczema

symptoms: dark spots on skin following inflammation (acne, eczema, trauma)
more common in darker skin types
slowly fades over months to years
guidance: Sun protection is essential. Topical tyrosinase inhibitors (hydroquinone, kojic acid, azelaic acid, retinoids). Chemical peels and laser may help. Avoid picking lesions. Be patient – resolution can take months.
precautions: Do not use hydroquinone for >3 months without breaks
If you have acne, treat it to prevent new PIH

symptoms: symmetrical, brown patches on the face (cheeks, forehead, upper lip)
worse with sun exposure and pregnancy
guidance: Sun protection is essential – use SPF 50+ (physical blockers). Topical hydroquinone, tretinoin, and corticosteroids (triple cream). Azelaic acid and kojic acid are alternatives. Chemical peels and laser for refractory cases. In pregnancy, may resolve after delivery.
precautions: Avoid oral contraceptives if they worsen
Do not use hydroquinone without breaks
If pregnant, avoid hydroquinone (use azelaic acid instead)

symptoms: associated with obesity, diabetes, and insulin resistance
guidance: If you have multiple skin tags, screen for diabetes and insulin resistance. Removal is cosmetic (cryotherapy, snip excision, or cautery). Prevention: weight loss and glycaemic control.
precautions: If you have many skin tags, check blood sugar
If you have diabetes, control it

symptoms: a conical, horn-like protrusion of keratin on sun-exposed skin (face, scalp, ears)
may be hard, yellowish, or brown
can be a precursor of squamous cell carcinoma at the base
guidance: Do not cut it at home. A dermatologist will shave it at the base and send for histopathology to rule out malignancy. Benign horns need no further treatment. If malignant, excise widely.
precautions: Do not pull or cut the horn
If you have a horn, see a dermatologist
If the base is indurated or ulcerated, it may be cancer
